sources.citation: Hyman, Larry M. 2017. Bantu Tone Overview. UC Berkeley PhonLab Annual Report 13 (printed pp. 162-177). doi:10.5070/P7131040751. (Published version: Hyman, Larry M. 2025. Tone. In The Oxford Guide to the Bantu Languages, 56-64. Oxford: OUP. doi:10.1093/oso/9780198808343.003.0006.)
sources.note: States that Ndamba [G52] is one of the relatively few Bantu languages lacking even a binary H vs. L tonal contrast, grouping it with Pogolo G51, Kutu, Kami, Zaramo, Kwere and Swahili in a non-tonal band running into Tanzania (sec. 1 'Tonal contrasts', p. 161). No further Ndamba data; no statement on where stress falls.

tone.quote: Most of the ca. 500 Bantu languages have at least a binary tonal contrast realized as surface H(igh) vs. L(ow). The relatively few exceptions include a discontinous band of languages starting in Mozambique with Sena [N44] and Nyungwe [N43], up around Lake Nyasa to Tumbuka [N21] and Nyakyusa [M31], and further East into Tanzania to Pogolo [G51], Ndamba [G52], Kutu [G37], Kami [G36], Zaramo [G33], Kwere [G32], and finally the best known case, Swahili (G42).
tone.locator: p. 161, section 1 'Tonal contrasts' (footnote 1 credits G. Philippson's input)
tone.summary: No lexical tone: Ndamba is listed among the Bantu languages that have lost the H/L tonal contrast (non-tonal, like neighbouring Pogolo and Swahili); the passage says nothing about stress placement.
tone.says: States that Ndamba [G52] is one of the relatively few Bantu languages lacking even a binary H vs. L tonal contrast, grouping it with Pogolo G51, Kutu, Kami, Zaramo, Kwere and Swahili in a non-tonal band running into Tanzania (sec. 1 'Tonal contrasts', p. 161). No further Ndamba data; no statement on where stress falls.
